::: {.prose}
Virality is defined as the concept of being quickly and widely spread or popularized, especially by means of social media ^[@mw_viral]. With TikTok entering the scene around 2018 as a short-form video platform and gaining major widespread popularity, the music industry experienced a massive shift ^[@stereofox_tiktok]. Tiny snippets of songs with catchy lyrics or fun beats, can be shared in a single video and reach millions of fans. This in turn spikes listening and streaming of the song. It has truly changed music marketing, discovery, and enjoyment. 

## What is the Billboard Hot 100? 

For some background, the Billboard Hot 100 is a music popularity ranking that originated in its current form in 1958 ^[@billboard_podcast]. Published weekly, it is a list of the most popular singles, originally based on radio airplay and the sales of the song, but now incorporates streaming data as well ^[@billboard_legend]. If you hear that a song is "Number 1," that means that it has reached the peak ranking of #1 on the Billboard Hot 100. This article examines the Billboard Hot 100 data from January 2016 to December 2025, for a total of 522 weeks, 5869 songs, and 1472 artists, scraped using billboard.py ^[@billboard_py]. 
:::

::: {.cr-wrapper}
::: {.cr-section}

These songs are examples of truly enduring hits that might not be the highest ranking song for all of its weeks on the chart, but they have consistent enough streams and sales in order to keep them in the top 100.

In order to capture the true lifecycle of a song's experience on the Billboard Charts, however, we need to dive into the rankings it achieves. The following chart depicts every single song that charted between 2016 and 2025, distributed vertically by their peak ranking and horizontally by the number of weeks they charted. This number of weeks value is based only on the charts gathered between January 2016 and December 2025, and does not include the number of weeks a song may have been on the chart either before or after those dates. This plot shows that a majority of songs chart for fewer weeks, with the songs from the previous bar graph as outliers along the top right edge of the grid. The number of weeks a song charts for ranges from 1 to 112, but fifty percent of songs chart for only 3 weeks or less. There is a clear trend in this scatter plot that shows as songs are on the chart for more weeks, their peak rank generally increases. In fact, this relationship has a positive correlation of about 0.6. The peak rank of a song is also positively correlated with it's debut rank: the higher a song debut's on the Hot 100, the higher it's peak ranking. Click on any point in the graph below to view its ranking over time. 
:::

::: {.chart-wrap}
```{python}
# imports 
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

# data 
df = pd.read_csv("../data/clean_hot100_history.csv", low_memory=False)
df_song_rank = df.copy()
df_song_rank = (
    df_song_rank
    .sort_values('chart_date')
    .groupby(['title', 'artist'], as_index=False)
    .agg(
        weeks_in_data=('chart_date', 'count'),
        peak_position=('rank', 'min'),
        debut_rank=('rank', 'first')
    )
)
# default_song = df.sort_values("weeks_on_chart", ascending=False).iloc[0]
df_filled = pd.read_csv("../data/filled_hot100_history.csv", low_memory=False)

# altair settings 
alt.data_transformers.disable_max_rows()
alt.renderers.enable('default', embed_options={'renderer': 'canvas'})

# custom color scale 
color_scale = alt.Scale(
    domain=[1, 50, 100],
    range=['#4f0335', '#882a9d', '#e4d1ee'],
)
@alt.theme.register('custom', enable=True)
def custom_theme():
    return alt.theme.ThemeConfig({
            "font": "Playfair Display, serif",
            "background": '#f5f0e8',
            "view": {
                "fill": '#f5f0e8',
                "stroke": "transparent",
            },
            "range": {
                "category": ['#4f0335', '#320b8d', '#06395b', '#6b2d0f', '#1a5c3a','#882a9d','#bd6220','#179191','#6b46c8'],
                "diverging": ['#4f0335', '#320b8d', '#06395b'],
                "heatmap": ['#e4d1ee', '#882a9d'],
            },
            "bar": {"color": '#320b8d'},
            "line": {"color": '#4f0335'},
            "point": {"color": '#4f0335'},
            
        }
    )

# scatter selection object 
selection = alt.selection_point(fields=["title", "artist"], empty=True)

# scatter plot
scatter = alt.Chart(df_song_rank).mark_circle(size=60).encode(
    x=alt.X("weeks_in_data:Q", title="Number of Weeks"),
    y=alt.Y("peak_position:Q", title="Peak Position", scale=alt.Scale(reverse=True)),
    color=alt.condition(
        selection,
        alt.Color("debut_rank:Q", scale=color_scale, legend=alt.Legend(title="Debut Rank", direction='horizontal', orient='bottom', gradientLength=700, tickCount=3)),
        alt.value("lightgray"),
    ),
    tooltip=[alt.Tooltip('title', title='Song'),
             alt.Tooltip('artist', title='Artist'),
             alt.Tooltip('weeks_in_data', title='Number of Weeks on Chart'),
             alt.Tooltip('peak_position', title='Peak Position'),
             alt.Tooltip('debut_rank', title='Debut Rank')],
).add_params(selection).properties(width=700, height=400, title=alt.Title(
       "Charting Time vs Peak",
       anchor='start',
       frame='group',
       orient='top',
       fontSize=16, 
       fontWeight='bold',
       offset=20
   ))

# decay curve selection object
curve_selection = alt.selection_point(fields=["title", "artist"], empty=False)

# add to scatter
scatter = scatter.add_params(curve_selection)

# decay curve 
curve = alt.Chart(df_filled).mark_line(point=True).encode(
    x=alt.X("chart_date:T", title="Week"),
    y=alt.Y("rank:Q", title="Chart Position", scale=alt.Scale(reverse=True)),
    color=alt.value('#4f0335'),
    tooltip=[alt.Tooltip('title', title='Song'),
             alt.Tooltip('artist', title='Artist'), 
             alt.Tooltip('chart_date:T', format='%b %d, %Y', title='Date'),
             alt.Tooltip('rank', title='Rank')],
).transform_filter(curve_selection).properties(width=700, height=300)
title = alt.Chart(df).mark_text(
    align='left',
    fontSize=16,
    fontWeight='bold'
).encode(
    text=alt.Text('title:N', aggregate='max')
).transform_filter(curve_selection)


combined = (scatter & title & curve).resolve_scale(color="independent").configure(font='serif')
combined
```
[In this chart and those that follow, debut rank refers to the song's rank on the first week in appears in the collected data. If a song was released and appeared on the Billboard Hot 100 prior to 2016, that debut is unfortunately not captured.]{.caption}
:::

:::{.prose}
Of course, the number of weeks a song charts can give us give us an initial view into if it is a viral flash or if its popularity endures, but a deeper dive looks at its rankings over time. If a song rapidly rises up the charts, it may be part of a viral trend on TikTok so more people are listening to it. If a song's rank remains relatively consistent over time or decreases very slowly, it could be a more sustained hit. See if you can fiddle with the plot above until you find a song that fits either of these categories. 

## How do we capture a flash or a burn?

In order to quantify a song's climb up the chart and its fall down it, I calculate rise and decay rates. Both of these metrics are calculated as the average of all weekly differences, where rise rate is positive and calcluated based on the weeks and ranks from a song's debut to its peak, and the decay rate is negative and is calculated from a song's peak to its last day on the chart. Put simply, they are slopes: the rise rate is the average number of ranks a song increases per week up until its peak, and the decay rate is the average number of ranks a song decreases per week after peaking. A rise rate of 0 means that a song debuts at its peak, and a decay rate of 0 means it ends at its peak. 

While these metrics provide a general assessment, they do have limitations. They only incorporate the initial ranking of a song, the peak ranking, the end ranking, and the number of weeks in between those points. Thus the rise and decay rates do not take into account the variability in a song's ranking before or after it reaches its peak. More influential for the decay rate calculations, songs that drop of the chart completely and then re-enter have extended post-peak lengths, and the final rank it ends on could be much higher than a lower rank it previously disappeared from. Thus the decay rate can appear very slow for a song that could have several flashes of popularity on the charts. 
:::

::: {.chart-wrap}
<iframe src="../../charts/rise_vs_decay.html" width=1000 height=600 style="border:none"></iframe>
[Diagram of song rise rate vs decay rate. Songs that only appear on the Billboard Hot 100 for a single week are not included.]{.caption}
:::

::: {.prose}
Using the chart above, we can do an initial categorization of flash vs burn songs. Songs in the bottom right quadrant are true "flash" songs that rise quickly up the rankings and then drop just as fast. For example, Taylor Swift's _Mr. Perfectly Fine (Taylor's Version)_ started at #90, peaked at #30 the next week, and then dropped back to #90 the next week and didn't reappear on the chart. Songs on the top right are viral hits, they climb quickly up the charts like the flashes, but they stick around and stay popular, with low decay rates. The bottom left corner is the opposite, they either debut at their peak if they lie on the vertical axis, or they have slow rises up the charts. Yet, their extreme decay rates mean that their popularity isn't sustainable and they rapidly drop in the rankings before falling off the chart. Most songs are clustered in the top left corner, with both slow rise rates and slow decay rates. 
:::

## Taylor Swift 


```{=html}
<div id="pathway-a" class="pathway">
```

::: {.pathway-header}
### Taylor Swift 
[Flash]{.artist-label}
:::

A major name in current pop music, Taylor Swift is the only artist to have won Album of the Year at the Grammys four times, and her 2023-2024 Eras Tour was the first concert tour to make $1 billion in revenue ^[@swift_records]. Her songs have been charting on the Billboard Hot 100 since her debut album in 2006. In the most recent decade, however, she has released 11 albums. The longest charting singles from those albums can be seen below. 

::: {.chart-wrap}
![](../../charts/timeline_taylor_swift.svg)
:::

Besides all of that, her single _ME!_ with Brendon Urie has the highest rise rate for any song in the Hot 100 between 2016 and 2025. In just one week, it rose from its debut rank at \#100 to \#2, for an increase of 98 ranks per week. Another viral rise was _Look What You Made Me Do_, from 2017's Reputation album. This was a surprise drop with no lead up marketing, and the song rose from a \#77 debut to \#1 in a single week. Previously mentioned was her song _Mr. Perfectly Fine (Taylor's Version)_, which also has a very high rise rate of 60 ranks per week. In the plot below, the top 20 of Taylor Swift's songs with the highest rise rates are shown. Each song's bar is colored by rank for the weeks since its first appearance on the chart in this time frame, where darker corresponds to a higher rank. Feel free to hover over the chart or zoom in to get a closer look. 

::: {.chart-wrap}
<div class="plot-container">
<iframe src="../../charts/heatmap_taylor_swift.html?v=1"></iframe>
</div>
:::

This next plot shows the distribution of the rise and decay rates for all of Taylor Swift's songs on the Hot 100 from 2016 to 2025. In the distribution plot, the rise rate has a large spike at 0, meaning a lot of her songs debut at their peak rank. There is a long tail to the right though, which indicates some outlier songs that have extremely fast jumps up the chart. The decay rate distribution of Taylor Swift's songs is less volatile, with a peak at around -10 and a tail out to about -87. Compared to other artists, Taylor Swift's songs have pretty fast decay rates, meaning that their popularity isn't sustained for long periods of time.

::: {.chart-wrap}
<div class="plot-container">
<iframe src="../../charts/violin_taylor_swift.html?v=1"></iframe>
</div>
:::

:::{.prose}
Taylor Swift's songs often debut at their peak or fly up the charts in a single week. These are viral, popular songs, but they don't always stick around. Explore another artist to see slow decays and long-lasting hits. 
:::

### Shawn Mendes
[Fade]{.artist-label}

::: {.prose}
Shawn Mendes is a great example of sustained hits. With 4 albums releasing between 2016 and 2020, you may remember his older music like _Stitches_ or _Senorita_ with Camilla Cabello, though he returned to music with his most recent album in 2024 ^[@shawn_mendes_wiki]. Though he has fewer songs on the Billboard Hot 100 than other artists explored here, his discography an interesting case in terms of slow decay. A timeline of his longest charting songs can be seen below. 
:::

::: {.chart-wrap}
![](../../charts/timeline_shawn_mendes.svg)
:::

In the heatmap below that shows selected songs with the slowest decay rates, you can see just how long Shawn Mendes's songs remain on the chart. Though _Treat You Better_ achieves the maximum of 39 total weeks, out of all his songs fifty percent chart for 16 weeks or more. This leads to him having one of the slowest average decay rates for artists with more than 10 songs. This cutoff for artists having more than 10 songs is important, since songs with the absolute smallest decay rates are usually one-off holiday songs that re-enter the charts each year. This extends the time frame over which decay is calculated and thus lowers the rate, though the song is probably only actively on the chart for a few weeks of the year. _Senorita_ has the slowest decay rate of Shawn Mendes's discography, averaging -1.5 ranks per week over 28 weeks after it peaked at #1. 
:::

::: {.chart-wrap}

Even just at a glance the spread is much smaller than for any of the other artists explored here. The decay rate distribution peaks at around -2.3, and has a mean of only -3.6 ranks per week. He also has a smaller rise rate distribution, with a mean of 1.6 and a maximum of only 6.5. 
:::

::: {.chart-wrap}
<div class="plot-container">

It is interesting that his songs are able to fade away like this in a world where attention spans are increasingly shorter and viral content is taking more precedence. 
:::

## How did virality change over time?

Now that you've seen some specific examples, let's dive into how these measures of popularity rise and fall changed over time. The era of this data has many influential moments, mainly the rise of TikTok and other short-form video sharing platforms, like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts ^[@bbc_tiktok]. This coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced everyone inside and made social media one of the main forms of human connection. 
:::

::: {.cr-wrapper}
::: {.cr-section}

This chart shows that 2020 was a major year for the Billboard Hot 100. Over 800 unique songs appeared on it, with 22 different songs reaching the number 1 spot. @cr-waffle

This breadth of music was not fully maintained, as the number of unique songs on the chart has fallen to back to 711 in 2025. 

That being said, there is still more turnover in music popularity after the pandemic and rise of TikTok, as compared to before.  

::: {#cr-waffle .cr-sticky}
::: {.chart-wrap}
![](../../charts/waffle.svg)
[Diagram of number of unique songs on the Billboard Hot 100 chart per year, where each small square represents a song.]{.caption}
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.prose}
Another interesting aspect of the Billboard Hot 100 over time is the percentage of songs that debut at their peak. These songs end up with a rise rate of 0, but they could very well have gone viral before hitting the chart. Since we don't have any data on the anticipation for songs before they are released or their popularity before they reach the Billboard Hot 100, the behavior of these songs remains an open question. 
:::

::: {.cr-wrapper}
::: {.cr-section}

What we do know, however, is that change of percentage of songs that debut on the Hot 100 Chart at their peak ranking is very similar to the trend of number of unique songs. @cr-percentage

In 2020, a maximum of about 71\% of songs debuted at their peak, compared to much smaller percentages beforehand, and similar but decreasing percentages after. 

::: {#cr-percentage .cr-sticky}
::: {.chart-wrap}
![](../../charts/percentage_debut_at_peak.svg)
[Diagram of the percentage songs per year that debut at their peak ranking.]{.caption}
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.prose}
This is important to keep in mind as we turn to the distribution of rise and decay rates over time. All of these songs with 0 rise rates skew the distributions further right as the years move on, suggesting that a full analysis of song virality would require more data than just the Billboard Hot 100 Rankings. That being said, the decay rate lower fences and first quartiles are lower especially after 2022. These faster decay rates would mean that more songs are dropping off the charts more quickly, which aligns with the increase of songs on the Hot 100 overall, which we saw above. 
:::

::: {.chart-wrap}
<iframe src="../../charts/rise_decay_per_year.html" width=1000 height=800 style="border:none"></iframe>
:::

<section id="conclusion">
  <div class="conclusion-inner">

    <h2>Virality vs Endurability</h2>

    <p style="color:#1a1a1a; font-size:0.9rem; line-height:1.6; max-width: 800px; margin-bottom:2rem;">
      While the Billboard Hot 100 Chart can give insight into a song or artist's success and popularity, many other things should be considered when measuring virality. Social media shares and anticipation for a song before it is released can make a song go viral before it even reaches the charts, where it can debut at its peak and flatten its rise rate metric to zero. Both rates span across chart re-entries and flucuations, not fully capturing the granular variability of song popularity up and down the charts. That being said, it is interesting to explore specific songs and artists, and I would be interested in furthering this analysis across with categories like song genre, artist gender, or song specifc features, as well as incorporate data from social media. 
    </p>

    <h2>What does the decade tell us?</h2>

    <div class="insight-grid">
      <div class="insight-card">
        <div class="insight-stat">↓27.9%</div>

      </div>

      <div class="insight-card">

      </div>
    </div>

    <p style="color:#1a1a1a; font-size:0.9rem; line-height:1.6; max-width:800px; margin-bottom:2rem;">
      In general, more songs come and go, as seen with the decrease in average weeks on the chart and general increase of unique songs, while the rarer hits dominate the top for longer, as seen with the increase in median weeks at #1. The overall rise rate trend doesn't necessarily indicate that songs are becoming more viral, though this could be affected by the increase in songs that debut at their peak. Because of this disparity, it would be interesting to compare rise and decay rates across the rankings, attempting to discover if higher peaking songs rise and fall faster or slower than songs that peak lower. 
    </p>
